one_liner: Schemaless JS-to-JS binary serializer that keeps object graphs and deduplicates repeated subtrees; much smaller than Protobuf on repetitive data.
what_it_does: JSBT.encode(value) turns a JS value into a compact tagged binary format. Supported values include plain objects, arrays, Map, Set, Date, BigInt, TypedArrays, global Symbols, class instances, undefined/NaN/-0, cycles and shared references. The output is a JS 'binary string' with one char per byte. JSBT.decode(string | string[] | number[]) restores the value with object identity intact, and JSBT.decodeStream(ByteStream) parses incrementally as chunks arrive. There is no schema, IDL or codegen. It is a structured-clone-style format for when both ends are JavaScript, not a Protobuf replacement for cross-language contracts. Class instances are encoded through toJSBT/toJSON/valueOf and can be rebuilt through a global JSBT.setClassFactories map.
how_it_is_fast: The size win comes from two dedup layers in the encoder, which is a form of content-addressed dedup or hash-consing. First, every value gets a ref ID, and a Map keyed by the value itself (object identity, or the value for longer strings, larger integers and floats) emits a short 'link' ref when that value appears again. Second, a Map keyed by each subtree's already-encoded bytes emits a 'copy' ref when an identical subtree was written before, but only if the ref is shorter than the bytes. Everything else is a 1-byte type/length tag followed by minimal little-endian bytes: variable-width integers, trimmed floats and UTF-8 strings. It is not faster: the encoder builds every subtree's encoding as a string and looks it up in a Map, which makes encoding about 10x slower than Protobuf on a flat object.
when_to_use: Both ends are JS/TS and you control both: Node to Node, Node to browser, Web Workers or worker threads, Electron IPC.

Payloads are large arrays of records in which many sub-objects or whole records are exact duplicates (logs, market or order-book snapshots, analytics exports). Here dedup can cut wire or storage size by an order of magnitude or more compared with JSON, Protobuf or MsgPack.
You need to round-trip JS types that JSON drops (Map, Set, Date, BigInt, TypedArrays, undefined, NaN, -0) or object graphs with cycles and shared references, with identity preserved.
Snapshotting in-memory state (caches, graphs) where size at rest matters more than CPU time spent encoding.
You want compact binary without maintaining .proto schemas or a codegen step.
when_not_to_use: Cross-language or schema-evolution contracts: the only implementation is TypeScript/JavaScript. Use Protobuf, Avro or Thrift, as the README itself advises.

Latency- or CPU-bound paths with small or flat messages. On the README's flat-object test JSBT is about 9.6x slower to encode than Protobuf (31.51 vs 3.29 us/op), about 10.7x slower to decode (20.83 vs 1.95 us/op), and also larger (1,398 vs 1,017 bytes).

Large payloads with few repeats. The encoder keeps every subtree's encoded string as a Map key, so encode time and memory grow with payload size. The README reports about 1,029 ms per encode for its 10,000-object repeated dataset.

Decoding untrusted input. A copy ref is expanded by re-decoding the referenced byte range, and the code I read has no expansion limit, so a small payload can decode into a very large heap. The README's security notes do not mention this.
When you need a small decoded heap. Copy refs decode into fresh objects, so structural dedup shrinks only the wire or stored form. Only same-identity (link) refs stay shared after decode.

integration.dependencies: none (runtime); devDependencies are the TypeScript, tsup and jest toolchain
integration.min_toolchain: ES2020 runtime (the tsup build targets es2020); TextEncoder is required for string encoding; package.json has no engines field; ships ESM and CJS builds with .d.ts typings
integration.platforms: any JS runtime; the README names Node, browsers, Web Workers and Electron
integration.thread_safety: not documented. encode and decode create fresh state on each call, but class factories are a process-global static set through JSBT.setClassFactories

gotchas: JSBT.encode returns a JS string with one char per byte (0-255), not a Uint8Array, and decode does not accept Uint8Array or ArrayBuffer. Byte output (encodeToBytes) and Uint8Array input exist only in the open, unmerged v1.4.0 PR #2. If the string goes through a UTF-8 path (for example Buffer.byteLength or a text frame), every byte at 0x80 or above becomes 2 bytes, so convert it as latin1/binary.
Integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER throw, so use BigInt for them. Local (non-global) symbol keys on objects are not encoded.

Any object whose constructor.name is not 'Object' is treated as a class instance and serialized through toJSBT(), toJSON() or valueOf(). On decode, a class name with no registered factory comes back as a plain object carrying a non-enumerable __jsbtConstructorName.
During decode, ByteStream keeps every input byte in a JS number array so that copy refs can re-parse their byte slices. Expect decode-time memory well above the payload size.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose JSBT over the catalog's other size-focused entries only when both endpoints are JavaScript and you want no schema plus graph and identity preservation. JSON BinPack gets its size wins from a schema and was the smallest or tied-smallest on 27 documents, and qdf reports wire-size wins over protobuf on 5 batch fixtures; both results are broader than JSBT's single dataset, which favours dedup.
verified_claims_summary: The size comparison with Protobuf comes only from README scenario 3: 10,000 repetitive objects encode, uncompressed, to 64,175 bytes with JSBT versus 3,108,000 with Protobuf (about 48x), 3,708,003 with MsgPack, 3,775,603 with CBOR and 4,680,335 with JSON. It was a single run 'on Node.js' with no Node version, hardware, or Protobuf library or schema stated, and the published harness (benchmarks/benchmark1.ts) runs only JSON and JSBT. In that harness's repeated dataset every field depends only on i mod 100 or i mod 3, so just 300 of the 10,000 records are distinct and the rest encode as short copy refs. The 48x therefore mostly measures whole-record dedup, not general compactness.
status_note: Actively maintained by one person: v1.3.2 was released 2026-04-05, and an open v1.4.0 PR since 2025-12 adds Uint8Array I/O. It is MIT-licensed with zero runtime dependencies and installable from npm, but adoption is low (36 stars, about 34 npm downloads a month) and there are no independent benchmarks.
